idiom_name: Mockito mock of the service interface (JDK dynamic proxy as the zero-dependency alternative)
implementation_notes: Mockito synthesizes the stand-in for an interface or non-final class - the default mock maker generates the implementation with Byte Buddy - and the mock is injected as the interface type, so the client is unaware; strict stubs flag unused or mismatched expectations. A zero-dependency realization is the JDK's own mechanism: Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, new Class<?>[]{PriceService.class}, handler) returns an object that implements the interface and routes every call through an InvocationHandler, which is exactly how RMI generates client stubs now that statically generated stubs are deprecated. For the production seam the stub comes from the IDL toolchain (gRPC, JAX-WS) and client code is unchanged.
pitfalls: The JDK dynamic proxy implements interfaces only and routes equals, hashCode and toString to the handler as well, so a handler that assumes business methods only will break collections, assertions and debugging.
Stubbings belong to a mock instance and to a test: a mock reused across tests carries its configured answers into the next one, so create mocks per test.
Mocking a final class or record requires an inline mock maker, and mocking a vendor type instead of an owned interface couples every test to a contract you cannot change.

variants.name: JDK dynamic proxy with an InvocationHandler (no library)
variants.implementation_notes: The standard library can build the stand-in itself: one handler sees every interface method as a reflected Method plus its arguments and can answer from a map of canned results - the same mechanism the RMI runtime uses to generate stubs dynamically. Choose it when no mocking library may be added (constrained dependency set, module system) and when the stand-in must answer many operations uniformly; choose Mockito when you need argument matching, verification and readable failure messages.
pitfalls: Returning null for an unhandled method silently satisfies the client, so make the default branch throw for every operation the stand-in does not model.
Checked exceptions declared by the interface must be rethrown through the handler; an undeclared one surfaces as UndeclaredThrowableException, which is easy to misdiagnose.

variants.name: RMI-generated stub bound to the naming service (legacy production seam)
variants.implementation_notes: The historical Java home of this pattern: the remote object is exported and the RMI runtime generates the client stub, which is a dynamic proxy implementing the remote interface, so the client holds the interface and calls it as a local object while the stub performs the remote invocation. Statically generated stubs are deprecated in favour of generation at export time, which is why the JDK's RemoteStub class is documented as deprecated while the proxy mechanism remains.
pitfalls: Every remote call can fail with RemoteException, so the real client contract is exception-rich: a stand-in that never throws hides exactly the failures the client must handle.
RMI's methods must be declared on a Remote interface, which constrains the design; a partial stand-in for a different interface type is not substitutable.
